practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct classification of the patella?
A) Long bone
B) Short bone
C) Flat bone
D) Sesamoid bone
practice_questions.marks: D) Sesamoid bone [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one bone in the lower leg and state its classification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: tibia (long bone) OR fibula (long bone). Accept either bone with its correct classification. No mark if classification is missing or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'bone density' and explain why weight-bearing exercise increases it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining bone density: the amount of mineral (calcium/phosphorus) per unit volume of bone, indicating bone strength. 1 mark for the explanation: weight-bearing exercise places mechanical load on bones, stimulating them to deposit more calcium/phosphorus into the bone matrix.

practice_questions.text: Describe two functions of the skeleton that are relevant to a rugby player during a match.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: identification of a function (1), sporting application (1) per function. Maximum 2 functions needed. Examples: protection — cranium protects the brain from impact during tackles (1+1); muscle attachment — the scapula provides a broad surface for shoulder muscles to generate the force needed for scrummaging (1+1); joints for movement — ball-and-socket shoulder joint allows the full circumduction needed to pass (1+1). Allow any two valid function + application combinations.

practice_questions.text: A county-level high jumper is reviewing her training plan. Explain why including weight-bearing exercises such as squats and box jumps would benefit the health of her skeleton, even though high jump itself is already an impact activity.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone remodelling (1); bones respond by increasing calcium and phosphorus deposition, increasing bone density (1); denser bones are more resistant to stress fractures (1); varied weight-bearing stimuli (squats, jumps at different angles) ensure loading across multiple bone regions rather than repetitive strain on one site (1). Maximum 4 marks. Credit any physiologically sound reasoning about the mineral storage or bone density function.

practice_questions.text: A sports scientist argues that understanding bone shape classification is essential for coaches designing injury-prevention programmes. Assess the extent to which knowledge of bone shape helps a coach reduce the risk of injury in a sport of your choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Clear, sustained argument linking specific bone shapes to specific injury risks in the named sport. Identifies at least three bone shape categories correctly. Reaches a supported judgement on extent. Consistent sporting application throughout. Example: in football, the patella (sesamoid) is vulnerable to patellar tendinopathy from overuse — a coach knowing this would periodise training to reduce repeated knee-extension loading; the tibia (long bone) is a lever that can fracture under bending force, so shin guards mitigate this; flat bones of the ribcage are at risk in aerial challenges. Concludes with a nuanced judgement e.g. 'knowledge of bone shape is highly useful for high-impact sports but coaches also need information on an individual player's bone density.'
Secure (3-4): Links bone shape to injury risk with mostly correct examples. Some sporting application. Partial judgement.
Developing (2): Correct bone classification but weak or absent injury-risk links. Limited sport context.
Emerging (1): Basic or isolated point about skeleton and injury with no clear structure.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes emotional health?
A) The absence of physical injury
B) The ability to manage feelings and respond to stress constructively
C) The ability to perform sport at a high level
D) The ability to form and maintain relationships
practice_questions.marks: B) The ability to manage feelings and respond to stress constructively [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify one physical health benefit and one social health benefit of regular participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any physical health benefit, correctly identified (e.g. improved cardiovascular fitness / reduced risk of coronary heart disease / improved body composition / reduced risk of obesity / increased bone density). 1 mark for any social health benefit, correctly identified (e.g. improved communication and cooperation skills / making friends / reduced social isolation / sense of belonging through team membership).

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular participation in sport can improve a person's emotional health.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for naming the mechanism (e.g. exercise triggers endorphin release); 1 mark for explaining the outcome (e.g. endorphins reduce anxiety and improve mood / create a sense of wellbeing); 1 mark for applying to a realistic sporting context (e.g. a swimmer who trains three times per week reports lower stress levels and better sleep quality as a result of the endorphin response during training).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old joins a local athletics club after a period of low mood and social isolation. Explain how club membership could improve two different dimensions of her health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for correctly identifying two different health dimensions (e.g. emotional + social). 1 mark each for explaining how the club addresses each dimension. Acceptable content: emotional — structured training goals and achievement of personal bests builds confidence and self-esteem; training triggers endorphin release reducing anxiety; social — training with peers builds friendships and a sense of belonging; shared goals in the team create cooperative bonds that reduce isolation.

practice_questions.text: A club-level cyclist has increased her training volume significantly over the past three months. Analyse the potential positive and negative effects of this increased training on her health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Positive and negative effects discussed across at least two health dimensions; each effect is linked to a specific mechanism (e.g. endorphin release for emotional benefit; overtraining causing fatigue/immune suppression as a negative); consistent application to the cycling context; technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Both positive and negative effects present; at least two health dimensions touched on; mostly accurate; cycling application present but may be general.

Developing: Either positive or negative effects discussed more fully; limited to one health dimension; some sporting application.

Emerging: Basic list of benefits or risks with little development or sporting application.

Acceptable positive content: improved cardiovascular fitness (reduced coronary heart disease risk); improved body composition; endorphin release improving mood; increased self-confidence as performance improves; social bonds with training partners.
Acceptable negative content: overtraining leading to physical exhaustion, increased injury risk; compulsive training can cause anxiety if rest feels impossible; pressure around body weight/composition in cycling can contribute to disordered eating; social withdrawal if training takes priority over other relationships.

practice_questions.text: A young athlete claims: ‘Sport is always good for your health — there are no downsides.’ Evaluate this statement, considering all three dimensions of health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full discussion across all three health dimensions (physical, emotional, social); balanced argument covering both benefits and risks; consistent sporting application; clear justified conclusion that challenges the athlete’s claim while recognising the genuine benefits.

Secure: At least two dimensions discussed; both benefits and risks present; some sporting application; conclusion present.

Developing: Mainly benefits discussed; limited to one or two dimensions; limited sporting application; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic list of health benefits with little or no discussion of risks or dimensions.

Agreeing (sport is good): physical benefits (cardiovascular fitness, reduced obesity/CHD/diabetes risk); emotional benefits (endorphin release, reduced anxiety, improved self-esteem); social benefits (teamwork, friendships, community belonging).

Disagreeing / partial challenge: overtraining can cause physical injury, fatigue and immune suppression; exercise addiction can increase anxiety rather than reduce it; social pressure in sport can lead to unhealthy body-image concerns and disordered eating; elite sport demands can isolate athletes from non-sporting social relationships.

Conclusion: Sport is broadly beneficial across all three health dimensions, but the benefits are maximised when training is balanced, goals are healthy, and participation is enjoyable rather than compulsive.

practice_questions.text: State one long-term consequence of a sedentary lifestyle on cardiovascular health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid cardiovascular consequence: increased risk of coronary heart disease / raised blood pressure / increased resting heart rate / increased risk of atherosclerosis.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sedentary lifestyle'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying lack of physical activity as the key feature (e.g. little or no regular exercise / predominantly inactive behaviour); 1 mark for contextualising with an example or the health consequence (e.g. typically involves prolonged sitting, screen time or desk-based work, leading to low energy expenditure and accumulation of excess body fat).

practice_questions.text: Describe how smoking reduces a performer's ability to sustain aerobic exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that carbon monoxide in smoke binds to haemoglobin, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; 1 mark for explaining that tar coats the alveoli, reducing the surface area for gas exchange and lowering the efficiency of oxygen absorption; 1 mark for stating the consequence for performance (the working muscles receive less oxygen, so the performer fatigues more quickly during sustained aerobic activity such as distance running).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows the average weekly hours of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for two groups of 16-year-old students. Group A: 5.8 hours. Group B: 0.9 hours. Interpret what this data suggests about the likely long-term health outcomes for students in Group B.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly reading the data (Group B averages only 0.9 hours, far below Group A's 5.8 hours and below recommended guidelines); 1 mark for identifying at least one physical health consequence for Group B (e.g. increased risk of obesity / coronary heart disease / type 2 diabetes / osteoporosis); 1 mark for identifying a mental health consequence (e.g. increased risk of depression or anxiety due to lack of endorphin release); 1 mark for a comparative or evaluative statement (e.g. Group B students are at significantly greater long-term health risk than Group A students across multiple health dimensions).

practice_questions.text: A secondary school introduces a daily 20-minute active break for all students in response to concerns about sedentary behaviour. Assess whether this intervention is likely to improve students' health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Factors supporting and questioning the intervention are weighed; health benefits explained with mechanisms (e.g. daily moderate activity raises heart rate, improves cardiovascular fitness, reduces obesity risk, triggers endorphin release improving mood); limitations acknowledged (e.g. 20 minutes may be insufficient; intensity matters; benefits depend on whether students are sedentary outside school); reasoned judgement reached.

Secure: Benefits and limitations both present; mostly accurate physiological explanation; reasoned conclusion.

Developing: Mainly benefits described; limited physiological mechanism; little evaluation of whether the intervention is sufficient.

Emerging: Basic statement that exercise is good with little development.

Acceptable content in support: daily activity raises heart rate and improves cardiovascular fitness over time; endorphin release improves emotional wellbeing; structured movement reduces prolonged sitting; social interaction during the break improves social health. Limitations: 20 minutes is relatively short; benefit depends on intensity; students may still be sedentary for the other 23+ hours; the intervention does not address diet or sleep.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which lifestyle choices are the most important factor in determining a person's long-term health outcomes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation across multiple lifestyle factors (diet, activity, sleep, alcohol/smoking); consideration of other determinants of health (genetics, socio-economic status, healthcare access); consistent sporting or health examples; justified conclusion that acknowledges lifestyle as highly important while recognising it is not the sole determinant.

Secure: At least three lifestyle factors covered; some acknowledgement of other health determinants; sporting examples present; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly lifestyle factors described with limited evaluation; other health determinants absent or minimal; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic list of lifestyle factors with no evaluative structure.

Agreeing (lifestyle is most important): diet, activity level, sleep and avoidance of alcohol/smoking account for the largest share of preventable disease; regular exercise reduces risk of CHD, obesity, type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis; smoking causes bronchitis/lung cancer; diet drives body composition.

Partial challenge: genetics influence susceptibility to disease regardless of lifestyle (e.g. familial hypercholesterolaemia); socio-economic factors limit access to healthy food and safe exercise spaces; access to healthcare affects early detection and treatment of disease. Conclusion: lifestyle choices are the single most modifiable and impactful factor for most people, but they interact with non-modifiable factors such as genetics and structural inequalities.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of cardiac muscle?
A) Under conscious control; attached to bones to produce movement
B) Found in blood vessel walls; controls vasoconstriction
C) Forms the heart wall; contracts involuntarily and rhythmically
D) Attaches to tendons; produces flexion and extension at joints
practice_questions.marks: C) Forms the heart wall; contracts involuntarily and rhythmically [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the muscle responsible for extending the knee and state which sport action this enables.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: quadriceps extend the knee — accept any valid sporting example such as kicking a ball, jumping, sprinting, cycling. No mark if only the sport action is given without the muscle name.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location and role of the latissimus dorsi in a swimming stroke.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for location: the large, broad muscle of the back, running from the lower spine/pelvis to the humerus. 1 mark for role: extends and adducts the humerus. 1 mark for sporting application: produces the powerful downward and backward pull of the arm through the water in freestyle/backstroke, propelling the body forward.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the deltoid and pectoralis major work together in a basketball chest pass, referring to the joint movements each muscle produces.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for deltoid: at the shoulder (ball-and-socket joint), the deltoid initially abducts the arm outward to receive the ball / can assist with horizontal flexion. 1 mark for pectoralis major: adducts and medially rotates the humerus, driving the arms forward to push the ball. 1 mark for linked explanation: the two muscles work in sequence — deltoid controls the arm position; pectoralis major generates the forward push that propels the ball.

practice_questions.text: A strength-and-conditioning coach is designing a lower-body training programme for a sprinter. Assess the relative importance of the gluteus maximus, quadriceps and hamstrings to sprint performance, and justify which one the coach should prioritise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Correctly identifies and describes the role of all three muscles in sprinting. Makes a supported comparative argument. Reaches a clear, justified conclusion on prioritisation. Example: gluteus maximus extends the hip, generating the rearward push that drives each stride forward; quadriceps extend the knee in the propulsive phase; hamstrings flex the knee to recover the leg and assist hip extension but are the most commonly strained muscle in sprinting. Concludes e.g. 'The gluteus maximus should be prioritised as it generates the largest propulsive force, though hamstring injury prevention is also critical.' Sustained sporting application.
Secure (3-4): Correctly identifies at least two muscles with mostly accurate roles. Some comparative argument. Partial conclusion.
Developing (2): Identifies muscles but roles are limited or vague. Little comparison.
Emerging (1): Names one muscle with a basic point.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows the muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) in cm² of three athletes before and after a 12-week resistance training programme.

Athlete | CSA before | CSA after
Lee     | 42         | 49
Marcus  | 38         | 47
Patrice | 45         | 52

Calculate the percentage increase in CSA for Lee.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: (49 - 42) / 42 × 100. 1 mark for correct answer with units: 16.67% (accept 16.7% or 17%). No mark if percentage sign is missing.

practice_questions.text: A distance runner consumes 3,000 kcal per day. If 57% of this comes from carbohydrates and each gram of carbohydrate provides 4 kcal, calculate how many grams of carbohydrate she consumes daily.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: 3,000 kcal x 0.57 = 1,710 kcal from carbohydrates; 1 mark for correct final answer with units: 1,710 ÷ 4 = 427.5 g of carbohydrate.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'hypertrophy' and explain why protein timing is important for power athletes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining hypertrophy: an increase in muscle fibre size resulting from resistance training. 1 mark for stating that protein provides the amino acids needed for muscle repair and growth after training. 1 mark for explaining the timing importance: consuming protein within 30-60 minutes after training maximises the muscle-repair response when fibres are most receptive to amino acid uptake.

practice_questions.text: Explain why even mild dehydration reduces an athlete's endurance performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that dehydration reduces blood volume; 1 mark for explaining that reduced blood volume increases blood viscosity, making blood thicker and harder to pump; 1 mark for linking this to the effect on performance (the heart must beat faster to maintain cardiac output, increasing perceived effort and causing earlier fatigue).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows the macronutrient intake of two athletes: Athlete A (sprinter) takes in 18% carbohydrate, 47% fat, 35% protein. Athlete B (marathon runner) takes in 65% carbohydrate, 20% fat, 15% protein. Interpret what this data suggests about how well each athlete's diet matches their sport's demands.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly reading/comparing the data (Athlete A is low in carbohydrate and very high in protein and fat; Athlete B has a high carbohydrate intake); 1 mark for assessing Athlete B's diet as appropriate (marathon running requires sustained aerobic effort fuelled by glycogen; 65% carbohydrate supports glycogen stores and delays fatigue); 1 mark for assessing Athlete A's diet as potentially problematic (sprinters also benefit from adequate carbohydrate for explosive anaerobic energy; 18% is below recommended levels and the very high fat intake is not optimal); 1 mark for a comparative evaluative statement (Athlete B's diet is better matched to sport demands; Athlete A may need to increase carbohydrate intake to optimise performance).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level hockey player wants to improve her body composition and sporting performance through dietary changes. Analyse the role of macronutrients in achieving her goals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All three macronutrients discussed with accurate roles and sport-specific application to hockey; timing of protein mentioned; carbohydrate loading not applicable here but appropriate carbohydrate fuelling for training discussed; energy balance considered; technically accurate language.

Secure: At least two macronutrients discussed with mostly accurate roles; hockey application present; some mention of quantity or timing.

Developing: One or two macronutrients described; limited sport application; limited analysis of how dietary changes achieve the specific goals stated.

Emerging: Basic statement that diet affects performance with little specific macronutrient detail.

Acceptable content: carbohydrates — primary fuel for the high-intensity sprinting and repeated efforts in hockey; adequate glycogen stores prevent mid-game fatigue; proteins — hockey involves physical contact and repeated muscle loading; post-training protein (within 60 min) promotes muscle repair and lean mass gain, improving body composition; fats — provide energy during lighter training days; essential for hormone production; unsaturated fats from healthy sources preferred; energy balance — she needs to expend slightly more than she consumes to lose fat while maintaining lean mass, avoiding too large a deficit which would impair recovery.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of carbohydrate loading for endurance athletes, considering both the evidence in favour and possible limitations of the strategy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of carbohydrate loading including the physiological rationale, the type of athlete it benefits, the specific protocol and the evidence of effectiveness; limitations discussed (not suitable for short events, can cause GI discomfort, requires tapering); balanced conclusion with a justified judgement.

Secure: Both benefits and limitations present; endurance context well developed; some physiological detail; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly benefits described with limited limitations; some physiological explanation; argument mainly descriptive.

Emerging: Basic description of carbohydrate loading with little evaluation.

In favour: maximises muscle and liver glycogen stores; delays the point of glycogen depletion ('hitting the wall') in events over 90 minutes; allows the athlete to maintain race pace for longer; particularly effective for marathon runners, cyclists and triathletes who perform for 2+ hours.

Limitations: not appropriate for events under 90 minutes (glycogen depletion is not the limiting factor); sprinters, team-sport players and gymnasts do not benefit significantly; some athletes experience gastrointestinal discomfort with very high carbohydrate intake; the strategy requires careful planning and coordination with taper; extra glycogen storage is accompanied by water retention (glycogen binds water), which can feel heavy and is a concern for weight-class or aesthetic sports.

Conclusion: carbohydrate loading is highly effective and evidence-based for the right athlete in the right event, but it is not a universal strategy and must be matched to the specific demands of the sport.

practice_questions.text:
During the downward phase of a squat (knee flexion), which muscle is acting as the antagonist?
A) Quadriceps
B) Hamstrings
C) Gastrocnemius
D) Gluteus maximus
practice_questions.marks: A) Quadriceps [1 mark]. During knee flexion the hamstrings are the agonist and the quadriceps are the antagonist.

practice_questions.text: State which muscle fibre type a 100 m sprinter would predominantly use and give one reason why.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Type IIx. 1 mark for reason: they produce the most explosive, powerful contractions needed for maximal sprint speed / they rely on anaerobic energy, appropriate for the short, high-intensity duration of a 100 m race.

practice_questions.text: Explain the roles of the biceps and triceps when performing a shot put release.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: at the moment of release the elbow is extending. 1 mark for: the triceps is the agonist, contracting to extend the elbow and drive the shot forward. 1 mark for: the biceps is the antagonist, relaxing to allow the extension to occur smoothly.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows the percentage of Type I muscle fibres in three athletes.

Athlete     | Sport              | % Type I fibres
Felicia     | 1500 m running     | 68%
Gareth      | 100 m sprint       | 24%
Harrison    | Football (midfield)| 51%

Interpret what the data shows about how fibre composition relates to sport demands.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: Felicia has the highest % Type I (68%) consistent with 1500 m being an aerobic endurance event requiring fatigue-resistant fibres (1+1). Gareth has the lowest (24%) consistent with sprinting requiring explosive Type IIx fibres for maximal anaerobic power (1+1). Harrison is intermediate (51%) reflecting football's mixed demands — repeated short sprints (Type II) interspersed with lower-intensity running (Type I) (1). Maximum 4 marks; credit any valid data quote + sporting implication combination.

practice_questions.text: A strength coach argues that knowing an athlete's muscle fibre composition is essential when designing a training programme. Assess this claim, referring to the properties of each fibre type and the implications for programme design.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Accurately describes all three fibre types with correct properties. Links each type to specific training methods (e.g. Type IIx benefits from plyometrics and maximal sprint intervals; Type I from continuous aerobic training). Identifies limitation: fibre ratio is largely genetic, so design must work with existing ratio. Reaches a supported judgement (e.g. 'knowing fibre composition is highly useful for setting training emphasis but should not be the only factor as technique, psychology and sport demands also matter'). Consistent sporting application.
Secure (3-4): Describes at least two types accurately with mostly correct links to training. Partial judgement.
Developing (2): Basic description of one or two types; limited training link.
Emerging (1): Simple point about muscles and training with no fibre type specificity.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'agonist' and give a specific example from a named sporting action.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for definition: the muscle that contracts to produce a desired movement at a joint (also accept: the prime mover). 1 mark for example: any correct pairing of muscle, movement and sport, e.g. quadriceps (agonist) contract to extend the knee during the kicking phase in football.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a closed skill?
A) Receiving a serve in badminton
B) Performing a vault in gymnastics
C) Tackling in football
D) Playing a drop shot under pressure
practice_questions.marks: B) Performing a vault in gymnastics [1 mark]. The vault is performed in a stable, predictable environment; the performer controls the timing and conditions without reacting to opponents or an unpredictable environment.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'open skill' and give one sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining open skill: a skill performed in a changing, unpredictable environment where the performer must adapt continuously. 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. tackling in rugby / receiving a badminton serve / dribbling past a defender in basketball / a football header contested by two players).

practice_questions.text: Explain why variable practice is more suitable than fixed practice for developing an open skill.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for defining or describing variable practice (the skill is rehearsed under different conditions and contexts); 1 mark for explaining the reason it suits open skills (open skills are performed in changing, unpredictable environments; variable practice develops the ability to adapt technique to different situations); 1 mark for applying to a sporting example (e.g. a footballer practises passing against one, two then three defenders so that they can adapt their execution to match conditions).

practice_questions.text: A coach is planning a training session for a beginner who is learning to perform a gymnastics vault. Using your knowledge of skill classification and practice structures, discuss the most appropriate approach.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly classifying the vault (closed skill, because the environment is stable and the performer controls the timing). 1 mark for assessing the vault's position on the organisation continuum (high organisation, as the run-up, hurdle, contact and flight must flow continuously and cannot easily be separated). 1 mark for recommending an appropriate practice structure (distributed practice, with rest intervals to prevent fatigue errors in a beginner). 1 mark for justifying the recommendation (beginners lack the strength and coordination to perform the vault well when fatigued; rest intervals allow the coach to give corrective feedback and maintain technique quality).

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old county-level netball player wants to improve her interception skill. Analyse how the classification of interception as an open skill should influence the practice structures her coach selects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Interception correctly identified as an open, complex skill (changing direction of the pass, reacting to opponent movement); organisation position discussed (medium-to-low, the movement and positioning can be separately rehearsed); variable practice justified with specific drill examples (1 v 1, 2 v 2, full game practice); distributed or variable practice defended over fixed; consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure: Open skill classification correct; variable practice recommended and justified; some organisation analysis; netball application present.

Developing: Open skill identified; practice type recommended with limited justification; limited analysis of organisation or why other practice types are less suitable.

Emerging: Basic label of skill type with little development of implications for practice.

Acceptable content: interception is open (the pass direction and opponent movement are unpredictable); variable practice is most appropriate as it mimics the changing conditions of a match; fixed practice would produce a defender who can only intercept when the pass comes at a predictable speed and angle (not useful in match play); distributed practice also appropriate as interception requires intense concentration and fatigued practice may embed poor timing habits.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of massed practice for developing sporting skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of massed practice with specific examples of when it is effective and when it is harmful; skill type (basic vs complex, closed vs open) used to justify when massed practice is/isn't appropriate; fatigue, motivation and error-embedding discussed; balanced conclusion.

Secure: Both advantages and disadvantages present; some skill-type contextualisation; examples used; conclusion present.

Developing: Either advantages or disadvantages more fully developed; limited skill-type contextualisation; argument mainly descriptive.

Emerging: Basic description of massed practice with little evaluation.

Advantages: efficient use of time; builds automaticity quickly through high repetition volume; well-suited to basic, closed skills that need to become habitual (e.g. a basketball free-throw, a gymnastic arabesque); mentally motivating for performers who want to feel they are doing lots of training.

Disadvantages: fatigue causes breakdown in technique, which risks embedding errors that are hard to correct; demotivating for learners or younger performers; not suited to complex or open skills where quality of practice matters more than quantity; performer may lose focus during extended repetition, reducing the cognitive engagement needed to truly learn the skill. Conclusion: massed practice is valuable in limited contexts (basic, closed skills, experienced performers who can maintain quality while fatigued) but is generally less effective than distributed practice for learning complex or open skills at GCSE level.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of the bicuspid valve?
A) It separates the left and right sides of the heart
B) It prevents backflow between the right atrium and right ventricle
C) It prevents backflow between the left atrium and left ventricle
D) It controls blood flow from the left ventricle into the aorta
practice_questions.marks: C) It prevents backflow between the left atrium and left ventricle [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old athlete has a resting heart rate of 65 bpm and a stroke volume of 75 ml. Calculate her resting cardiac output.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: Q = 75 ml × 65 bpm. 1 mark for correct answer with units: 4,875 ml/min (accept 4.875 L/min). No mark if units are missing or if formula is not shown.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of vascular shunting during exercise and explain its importance for performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for what vascular shunting is: redistribution of blood flow from non-essential organs to working muscles during exercise. 1 mark for the mechanism: arterioles supplying non-essential organs vasoconstrict; arterioles in working muscles vasodilate. 1 mark for the performance importance: ensures working muscles receive a much greater proportion of the increased cardiac output, maximising oxygen delivery and waste removal.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows heart rate and stroke volume data for a recreational runner at rest and at three exercise intensities.

Condition        | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
Rest             | 70               | 70
Light exercise   | 100              | 85
Moderate exercise| 145              | 110
Maximal exercise | 190              | 120

Calculate the cardiac output at maximal exercise and compare it to resting cardiac output.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for maximal cardiac output calculation: 190 × 120 = 22,800 ml/min (22.8 L/min). 1 mark for comparison with resting: resting Q = 70 × 70 = 4,900 ml/min; maximal is approximately 4.7 times greater / an increase of about 17,900 ml/min. Accept correct figures based on the data given.

practice_questions.text: Explain the sequence of blood flow through the heart during one cardiac cycle, naming all chambers, valves and major vessels.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for correctly sequencing: deoxygenated blood enters right atrium via vena cava (1); passes through tricuspid valve into right ventricle, then out via pulmonary artery to lungs (1); oxygenated blood returns via pulmonary vein to left atrium, passes through bicuspid valve into left ventricle, exits through aorta to the body (1). Deduct no marks if semi-lunar valves are not mentioned, but credit if included.

practice_questions.text: A school swimming coach claims that cardiovascular fitness is the most important component of fitness for a 400 m swimmer. Assess this claim, referring to the structure and function of the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Strong case for cardiovascular fitness: a 400 m swim lasts approximately 4 minutes at high intensity, requiring sustained aerobic energy; the cardiovascular system must maintain high cardiac output (high SV and HR), effective vascular shunting to arm and leg muscles, and efficient gas exchange via dense capillary networks. Counterargument: muscular endurance and technique efficiency also matter. Structured judgement: e.g. 'cardiovascular fitness is the primary limiting factor at 400 m — the aerobic system dominates, and a well-trained heart increases stroke volume and therefore sustained cardiac output — but it is not the only factor.' Technical language throughout.
Secure (3-4): Correct links between cardiovascular function and swimming endurance. Partial counterargument or no clear judgement.
Developing (2): Basic points about heart rate or oxygen delivery without developed reasoning.
Emerging (1): Vague reference to heart and exercise.

practice_questions.text: Identify the letter in the SMART acronym that specifies a deadline for achieving the goal.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: T / Time-bound.

practice_questions.text: A swimmer has set the following goal: 'I want to swim better.' Explain two ways in which this goal fails the SMART criteria.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two valid SMART failures correctly identified and briefly explained: Not Specific (does not name which stroke, distance or aspect of swimming to improve); Not Measurable (no numerical or observable criterion to judge success); Not Time-bound (no deadline for achieving the goal); could also argue Not Achievable as it cannot be evaluated.

practice_questions.text: Explain how SMART goal setting can improve a performer's motivation during a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for explaining that specific, measurable goals show the performer exactly what to work towards, focusing their effort; 1 mark for explaining that short-term milestones that are achievable provide regular feelings of accomplishment, maintaining motivation; 1 mark for explaining that time-bound goals create urgency and allow the performer to track progress, giving a sense that the effort is producing results.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club tennis player wants to improve his first-serve accuracy. Write a SMART target for him and explain how it meets each criterion.
practice_questions.marks: A model answer: 'I will improve my first-serve accuracy from 50% to 70% in competitive match play by the end of the 6-week pre-season training block, by completing three serve-focused sessions per week.' 1 mark for Specific (first-serve accuracy named); 1 mark for Measurable (50% to 70%); 1 mark for Achievable and Realistic (a 20-percentage-point improvement in 6 weeks is challenging but plausible for a dedicated club player, and it is relevant to his tennis performance); 1 mark for Time-bound (6-week pre-season block). Other valid SMART targets can be credited if all five criteria are present and the target applies to the player described.

practice_questions.text: Assess the extent to which goal setting is the most effective psychological strategy for improving sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Goal setting's benefits explained with mechanisms (direction, motivation, evaluation); compared against other psychological strategies (mental rehearsal, arousal control, focus cues); relative importance reasoned; conclusion reached with justification.

Secure: Benefits of goal setting explained accurately; one or two other strategies compared; reasoned conclusion.

Developing: Goal setting benefits described; limited comparison with other strategies; argument mainly descriptive; conclusion may be present but not fully reasoned.

Emerging: Basic description of SMART goals with little analysis or comparison.

Acceptable content: goal setting benefits — directs training, sustains motivation, enables evaluation, supports intrinsic motivation when self-set; limitations — goals alone do not improve physical capability; a performer also needs effective mental rehearsal for arousal control, attentional focus strategies (cue words, pre-performance routines) and effective coaching. Conclusion: goal setting is a foundational psychological strategy and should underpin any training programme, but it achieves maximum effect when combined with other mental skills training.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effective SMART goal setting is in improving long-term athletic performance, considering both its strengths and limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of goal setting covering strengths (direction, motivation, evaluation, intrinsic motivation, short/long-term structure) and limitations (goals can be set unrealistically by coaches rather than performers, reducing ownership; goals can become demotivating if consistently unmet due to injury; outcome goals outside the performer's control; SMART criteria can be met on paper but be poorly calibrated); consistent sporting examples; balanced conclusion.

Secure: Both strengths and limitations present; at least two sporting examples; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly strengths described; limited limitations; some sporting examples; largely descriptive.

Emerging: Basic description of SMART goals with little evaluation.

Strengths: all five SMART criteria have evidence-based rationale; specific goals direct practice; measurable goals enable evaluation; achievable goals build confidence; time-bound goals create urgency; short-term goal ladders maintain motivation.

Limitations: goal setting is only as effective as the goal itself; poorly set goals (either too easy or impossible) undermine confidence; goals imposed by coaches without athlete input reduce intrinsic motivation and ownership; injury, illness or life events may make even well-crafted goals temporarily unrealistic; a performer fixated on a specific goal may lose enjoyment in sport if they repeatedly fall short. Conclusion: SMART goal setting is one of the most powerful and accessible psychological tools for improving long-term performance, but it requires regular review, athlete input and calibration to remain effective.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of the alveoli?
A) They are the main airways conducting air into the lungs
B) They are the sites of gas exchange between air and blood
C) They are the muscles that inflate the lungs during breathing
D) They store inhaled air before it reaches the bronchioles
practice_questions.marks: B) They are the sites of gas exchange between air and blood [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the approximate percentage of oxygen in inhaled air and in exhaled air.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for inhaled: approximately 21% oxygen. 1 mark for exhaled: approximately 16% oxygen. Accept values within ±1% of these figures.

practice_questions.text: Describe the mechanics of inhalation, naming the muscles involved and explaining why air enters the lungs.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for diaphragm: contracts and flattens, increasing the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. 1 mark for external intercostals: contract and lift the ribcage upward and outward, increasing the lateral dimension. 1 mark for pressure explanation: increased thoracic volume reduces air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air moves in from outside down the pressure gradient.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows tidal volume and breathing rate data for a club cyclist at rest and during three stages of a training session.

Stage            | Tidal volume (L) | Breathing rate (breaths/min)
Rest             | 0.5              | 14
Warm-up          | 1.2              | 20
Moderate effort  | 2.1              | 28
Maximal effort   | 2.9              | 38

Calculate the total volume of air breathed per minute (minute ventilation) at rest and at maximal effort.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for rest: 0.5 × 14 = 7.0 L/min. 1 mark for maximal: 2.9 × 38 = 110.2 L/min. Accept correct arithmetic based on the figures given. Units (L/min) required.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the alveoli are well-adapted for efficient gas exchange during high-intensity exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for large surface area: millions of alveoli create a very large total surface area for diffusion. 1 mark for thin membrane: the combined alveolar and capillary wall is only two cells thick, minimising diffusion distance. 1 mark for rich blood supply: dense network of pulmonary capillaries maintains a steep concentration gradient by constantly removing O2 and delivering CO2.

practice_questions.text: A personal trainer is advising a client who has recently completed a course of respiratory physiotherapy following a lung infection. The client is now returning to exercise. Assess the extent to which the respiratory system limits exercise performance compared to the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Accurately describes the role of the respiratory system (tidal volume, gas exchange, breathing mechanics) and the cardiovascular system (cardiac output, oxygen transport, vascular shunting). Makes a comparative argument: in healthy individuals, the cardiovascular system is usually the primary limiting factor at maximal intensity because cardiac output determines O2 delivery; the respiratory system has surplus capacity. However, in a person recovering from lung infection, reduced alveolar surface area, reduced vital capacity or obstructed airways could make the respiratory system the limiting factor. Reaches a supported, nuanced judgement. Consistent sporting/clinical application.
Secure (3-4): Identifies roles of both systems with mostly correct physiology. Some comparison. Partial judgement.
Developing (2): Describes one system adequately; the other is limited or missing.
Emerging (1): Basic mention of breathing or heart with no comparative analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following describes manual guidance?
A) A coach explaining the technique verbally
B) A performer watching a video of themselves
C) A coach physically moving the performer through the movement
D) Using a harness to support aerial work
practice_questions.marks: C) A coach physically moving the performer through the movement [1 mark]. Option D describes mechanical guidance (apparatus); option A is verbal; option B is visual.

practice_questions.text: Define 'concurrent feedback' and give one sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly defining concurrent feedback: information given during the performance of a skill as the movement is happening. 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. a swimming coach calling corrections from the poolside as the swimmer completes a training length / a dance teacher calling adjustments while students perform a routine).

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of visual guidance when teaching a beginner a new sport skill.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for stating an advantage of visual guidance (e.g. it gives the beginner a clear cognitive model of what the correct movement looks like, which is essential when they have no prior experience of the skill); 1 mark for stating a disadvantage (e.g. an expert-level demonstration may be too fast or technically advanced for a beginner to process, leading to cognitive overload); 1 mark for applying both points to a specific sporting scenario (e.g. showing a beginner a full-speed gymnastics vault demonstration may confuse rather than guide them, whereas a slower, broken-down demo would be more effective).

practice_questions.text: A club badminton coach is working with a 14-year-old beginner learning the overhead clear. Discuss whether verbal or visual guidance is more appropriate at this stage of learning.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining or describing each guidance type in the context (verbal: spoken instruction such as 'hit high and deep'; visual: demonstration of the stroke by the coach or video). 1 mark for arguing in favour of visual guidance for this beginner (the learner does not yet have a cognitive model of the overhead clear; a demonstration provides a complete picture of the movement; beginners benefit from seeing before being told). 1 mark for arguing limitations of verbal guidance for this learner (a beginner may not yet have the kinaesthetic vocabulary to translate complex verbal instructions into physical movement). 1 mark for a justified conclusion (visual guidance is likely more appropriate initially because it provides the mental model the beginner needs before verbal cues can be meaningful; verbal guidance can be added as a refinement tool once the basic pattern is established).

practice_questions.text: A county-level netball coach provides feedback to players during and after matches. Analyse the relative value of concurrent and terminal feedback for improving player performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both feedback types clearly defined; advantages and disadvantages of each discussed with accurate physiological or psychological reasoning; consistent application to netball; comparative analysis; conclusion reached.

Secure: Both types defined; advantages of each present; mostly applied to netball; some comparison; conclusion present.

Developing: One feedback type more fully analysed; limited comparison; some sporting application.

Emerging: Basic description of the two types with little analysis or application.

Acceptable content: concurrent advantages — immediate correction prevents errors from being repeated within the same session; particularly useful for technical cues during lower-intensity drills; concurrent disadvantages — can distract a player during a high-pressure match situation; complex concurrent instructions may overload working memory during fast-paced play; terminal advantages — allows considered, detailed review after match footage; performer is not distracted during play; can be supported by video; terminal disadvantages — delay between movement and information makes it harder to connect the feedback to the specific action; player memory of the relevant moment may have faded. Conclusion: both types have a role; concurrent feedback is valuable during training drills; terminal feedback is best for post-match analysis of patterns and tactical decisions.

practice_questions.text: A gymnastics coach works with performers at different stages of learning. Evaluate which guidance and feedback strategies are most effective for beginners compared to advanced performers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation contrasting beginners (visual, manual, mechanical guidance; extrinsic, terminal feedback) with advanced performers (verbal cue words, minimal mechanical support; intrinsic, concurrent feedback); mechanisms explained (beginners lack kinaesthetic awareness; advanced performers can interpret their own sensations); consistent gymnastics application throughout; balanced, justified conclusion.

Secure: Both learner stages addressed; at least two guidance and two feedback types compared; generally accurate; some gymnastics application; conclusion present.

Developing: One stage more fully developed; limited feedback comparison; some sporting application.

Emerging: Basic description of guidance or feedback with little comparison of learner stages.

Beginners: visual (demonstration of vault or routine gives a cognitive model); manual (coach physically supporting learner through a forward roll prevents injury and establishes feel); mechanical (harness in aerial work removes fear); extrinsic (coach provides objective information the beginner cannot generate internally); terminal (post-drill review is less disruptive than concurrent instructions during a fragile beginner movement).

Advanced: verbal cue words (minimal distraction, triggers trained movement patterns); rely more on intrinsic feedback (tuned kinaesthetic sense from years of practice); concurrent feedback from a specialist coach may be valuable for subtle corrections; less reliance on mechanical support which would alter the movement dynamics. Conclusion: guidance and feedback selection must be matched to the learner’s stage; what helps a beginner internalise a new skill can actually hinder an advanced performer who has already automated their technique.

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique an athlete can use to lower their arousal before competing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: deep breathing / controlled breathing / progressive muscle relaxation / positive self-talk / mental rehearsal / imagery (accept any valid arousal-reduction technique named without explanation).

practice_questions.text: Define 'mental rehearsal' and give one example of how a gymnast might use it before a competition.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly defining mental rehearsal: a cognitive technique in which the athlete mentally simulates a performance or skill in detail without physically executing it. 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. a gymnast mentally walks through their floor routine, visualising each element in sequence, including the timing, the feel of each movement and a successful landing, in the warm-up area before their turn).

practice_questions.text: Explain how deep breathing helps a performer reduce anxiety before competing.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that deep breathing involves deliberately slowing and deepening the breath; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (slow, deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system, counteracting the adrenaline-driven stress response and lowering heart rate and muscle tension); 1 mark for applying to a sporting example (e.g. a penalty-taker who takes two slow, deep breaths before their run-up is lowering their arousal to the level needed for the precise motor control that penalty-taking requires).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level archer experiences high anxiety before competitions, leading to trembling and loss of concentration. Discuss two mental preparation strategies her coach could recommend.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for naming two valid strategies (e.g. progressive muscle relaxation + positive self-talk). 1 mark each for explaining how each strategy addresses the specific problem described. Acceptable content: progressive muscle relaxation — systematically tensing and releasing muscle groups releases the somatic tension that causes trembling; the archer practises this in the warm-up area before competing; positive self-talk — replaces the negative internal dialogue ('I will miss') with process-focused cues ('breathe, anchor, release') that redirect attention from anxiety to technique, addressing the concentration loss.

practice_questions.text: A club-level sprinter uses mental rehearsal as part of her pre-competition warm-up. Analyse how mental rehearsal can improve her performance at a county athletics meeting.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mental rehearsal clearly defined; mechanisms explained (motor programme reinforcement, confidence building, arousal regulation, attentional control); consistently applied to sprinting performance; both the psychological and potential physiological mechanisms considered; technically accurate language.

Secure: Mental rehearsal defined; at least two mechanisms explained; mostly applied to sprinting; generally accurate.

Developing: Mental rehearsal described; one or two mechanisms mentioned; limited analysis of how it specifically improves sprinting performance.

Emerging: Basic description of mental rehearsal with little analysis.

Acceptable content: reinforces the motor programme for the sprint start without physical fatigue; builds confidence by mentally experiencing a successful start and race; helps regulate arousal to the high level required for a sprint without tipping into over-arousal; narrows attentional focus to the start signal and drive phase; the sprinter arrives at the blocks having already “run” the race successfully in her mind, reducing the novelty and unpredictability of the competition environment.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which mental preparation strategies can improve sporting performance, considering evidence both for and against their effectiveness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of mental preparation strategies (mental rehearsal, imagery, arousal management, pre-performance routines); evidence of effectiveness discussed; limitations acknowledged (strategies require practice to be effective; novices may lack the kinaesthetic experience to make imagery meaningful; high anxiety may overwhelm technique-based strategies; other factors such as physical fitness and tactical knowledge also determine performance); consistent sporting examples; balanced, justified conclusion.

Secure: At least two strategies discussed with evidence of effectiveness; some limitations present; sporting examples used; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly benefits described; limited limitations; some sporting examples; argument largely one-sided.

Emerging: Basic description of mental preparation with little evaluative content.

For effectiveness: mental rehearsal + physical practice produces better outcomes than physical practice alone; arousal management enables performers to reach optimal states for specific tasks; pre-performance routines shown to stabilise performance under pressure; widely used by elite performers (consistent, structured routines before major events).

Against: strategies require long practice to work; novices may be unable to create meaningful imagery because they lack the kinaesthetic experience; no strategy eliminates the physical and tactical factors that also determine outcome; under extreme competition pressure, even well-practised routines can break down; not equally effective for all performers or all sports. Conclusion: mental preparation is an evidence-supported and important component of performance, particularly at elite level, but it is most effective as part of a comprehensive preparation that includes physical training, tactical knowledge and competition experience.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct word equation for anaerobic respiration?
A) Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
B) Glucose → lactic acid + energy
C) Fat + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
D) Glucose → carbon dioxide + energy
practice_questions.marks: B) Glucose → lactic acid + energy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per correct difference, maximum 2. Accept any two of: aerobic requires oxygen / anaerobic does not; aerobic produces CO2 and water as by-products / anaerobic produces lactic acid; aerobic produces more ATP per glucose / anaerobic produces less; aerobic can be sustained longer / anaerobic fatigues within 1-2 minutes; aerobic uses fats and glucose / anaerobic uses glucose only.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old athlete wants to train in her aerobic zone. Using the simplified formula, calculate her maximum heart rate and then calculate the lower and upper limits of her aerobic training zone.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for max HR: 220 − 16 = 204 bpm. 1 mark for aerobic zone: lower limit = 204 × 0.60 = 122.4 bpm; upper limit = 204 × 0.80 = 163.2 bpm (accept rounded values). Both limits needed for full mark. Units (bpm) required.

practice_questions.text: Explain why lactic acid accumulates in the muscles of a 400 m runner in the final 100 m of a race.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for what happens: the runner sustains a high running speed that demands more energy than the aerobic system can supply. 1 mark for the mechanism: insufficient oxygen reaching the muscles means glucose cannot be fully oxidised aerobically; anaerobic respiration occurs, producing lactic acid as a by-product. 1 mark for the consequence: lactic acid accumulates faster than it can be cleared, interfering with muscle contractions and causing fatigue/burning sensation in the legs.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows heart rate data for two athletes (A and B) performing the same 30-minute moderate-intensity run.

Time (min) | Athlete A HR (bpm) | Athlete B HR (bpm)
0           | 65                 | 80
5           | 148                | 162
15          | 152                | 170
30          | 150                | 168

Athlete A is a trained endurance runner; Athlete B is untrained. Interpret what the data shows about the effect of training on cardiovascular response to exercise.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: Athlete A has a lower resting HR (65 vs 80 bpm) consistent with training-induced bradycardia (1). Athlete A reaches a lower exercise HR (148–152 vs 162–170 bpm) at the same workload, suggesting a higher stroke volume delivers sufficient cardiac output at a lower heart rate (1). The difference in exercise HR (~16–18 bpm lower in A) means Athlete A is working at a lower relative intensity and is therefore more likely to be in the aerobic zone (1). Quote specific figures from the table to support each point (1). Maximum 4.

practice_questions.text: A sports science tutor argues that most competitive sports primarily use aerobic respiration and that anaerobic training is overrated. Assess this claim, using specific sport examples and your knowledge of energy systems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Acknowledges truth in claim — many sports are aerobically dominated (e.g. 10,000 m running, cycling, triathlon). Challenges claim with specific anaerobic examples: team sports (football, basketball) require frequent maximal sprints relying on anaerobic glycolysis; power events (shot put, 100 m) are almost entirely anaerobic. Points out that even 'aerobic' sports require anaerobic capacity for tactical surges (marathon finishing kicks, cycling attacks). Reaches a judgement: 'The claim oversimplifies; most sports require both systems, and the optimal ratio depends on the event demands.' Specific data or % energy system split strengthens the answer.
Secure (3-4): Identifies both systems with mostly correct sport examples. Makes a partial judgement.
Developing (2): Describes one system adequately with a sport example; comparison is limited.
Emerging (1): Basic mention of aerobic/anaerobic without sport application or comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct definition of the anticipatory rise?
A) The rise in cardiac output that occurs during maximal exercise
B) The rise in heart rate that occurs before exercise begins in response to anticipated effort
C) The increase in stroke volume during exercise due to greater venous return
D) The rise in lactic acid before the lactate threshold is reached
practice_questions.marks: B) The rise in heart rate that occurs before exercise begins in response to anticipated effort [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old athlete has a heart rate of 88 bpm and a stroke volume of 82 ml at the start of exercise. Calculate her cardiac output at this point.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: Q = 88 × 82. 1 mark for correct answer with units: 7,216 ml/min (accept 7.216 L/min). Units required.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows heart rate and stroke volume data for a club-level athlete at rest and during a 20-minute interval training session.

Phase            | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
Rest             | 58               | 80
Warm-up (5 min)  | 115              | 95
Interval 1       | 182              | 120
Recovery         | 130              | 98
Interval 2       | 178              | 118

Calculate the cardiac output during Interval 1 and compare it to resting cardiac output.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for Interval 1: 182 × 120 = 21,840 ml/min. 1 mark for comparison: resting Q = 58 × 80 = 4,640 ml/min; cardiac output during interval 1 is approximately 4.7 times greater, an increase of about 17,200 ml/min. Both calculations must include units. Accept correct arithmetic.

practice_questions.text: Explain the short-term effects of exercise on breathing rate and depth, and why both changes are necessary for performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for rate increase: breathing rate rises (from ~15 to up to 60 breaths/min) in response to rising CO2 detected by chemoreceptors, signalling the respiratory centre to increase breathing frequency. 1 mark for depth increase: tidal volume increases (~0.5 L to ~3 L) as diaphragm and intercostals contract more forcefully. 1 mark for why both are needed: increasing rate alone results in shallow breathing that doesn't fully reach the alveoli; increasing depth ensures more air enters the alveoli where gas exchange actually occurs, maximising oxygen uptake.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to lactic acid during high-intensity exercise and explain how this affects a performer during a 400 m race.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for description: lactic acid accumulates when exercise intensity exceeds the lactate threshold — anaerobic respiration rate outpaces the body's ability to remove lactic acid. 1 mark for physiological effect: lactic acid build-up in the muscles interferes with muscle contractions, causing the burning sensation and heavy-legged fatigue. 1 mark for performance effect: the 400 m runner must reduce speed or risks a dramatic decline in performance, particularly in the final 100 m when glycogen stores deplete and lactic acid peaks.

practice_questions.text: A university sports scientist is studying the short-term effects of exercise on two groups: trained endurance athletes and untrained individuals. She measures heart rate, stroke volume and lactate at rest and during a standardised 15-minute run at the same absolute speed. Assess the likely differences between the two groups and explain what these differences tell us about the value of aerobic training.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Predicts lower resting and exercise HR in trained athletes (bradycardia + higher SV means same cardiac output at lower HR). Trained athletes have higher stroke volume, meaning they can deliver the same cardiac output with fewer beats. Trained athletes have a higher lactate threshold, so accumulate less lactic acid at the same absolute speed, meaning they work at a lower relative intensity. Reaches a supported judgement: 'These differences demonstrate that aerobic training improves the efficiency of the cardiovascular system and extends the range within which the body can sustain aerobic energy production — both of which directly improve endurance performance.' Consistent data-referenced or sport-referenced application.
Secure (3-4): Correct comparisons on at least two measures. Partial explanation of training value.
Developing (2): One correct comparison without clear training explanation.
Emerging (1): Basic point about trained vs untrained hearts.

practice_questions.text: Identify one barrier to sport participation faced by people from lower socio-economic groups.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid cost or access barrier: high cost of club fees or specialist equipment / lack of affordable local sport facilities / transport costs to facilities / inability to afford private coaching.

practice_questions.text: Describe two factors that have led to an increase in female participation in sport over recent decades.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two valid factors, correctly described: increased media coverage of women's sport (e.g. Women's World Cup) raising awareness and creating role models; high-profile female athletes challenging gender stereotypes and inspiring participation; increase in women-only sport provision removing perceived barriers; national campaigns and funding directed at women's sport; greater social acceptance of women competing across all sport types.

practice_questions.text: Explain how disability can create barriers to participation in physical activity and sport.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying a physical/structural barrier (e.g. inaccessible facilities without ramps or adapted equipment); 1 mark for identifying a psychological barrier (e.g. low confidence, fear of injury or experience of exclusion in mainstream sport settings); 1 mark for applying to a realistic sporting context (e.g. a wheelchair user may find that their local leisure centre lacks accessible changing facilities, and may also feel unwelcome in mainstream group exercise classes that are not designed for participants with mobility impairments).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows weekly sport participation rates by age group: 16-24: 62%. 35-54: 38%. 65+: 21%. Interpret what this data suggests about how age affects engagement patterns in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly reading the data (participation declines progressively with age, from 62% in the 16-24 group to 21% in those aged 65+). 1 mark for identifying a reason for decline among the middle age group (35-54: competing demands from work, family and reduced time for sport). 1 mark for identifying reasons for the lowest participation among 65+ group (reduced mobility, chronic health conditions, fear of injury, lack of age-appropriate provision). 1 mark for a comparative or evaluative statement (the 41-percentage-point difference between the youngest and oldest groups indicates significant age-related inequality in engagement, which targeted programmes such as walking football and community swimming sessions could address).

practice_questions.text: Assess the effectiveness of using role models to increase sport participation among underrepresented groups.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Role models' effectiveness evaluated with reasoning; specific examples of role models given; evidence of impact on participation considered; limitations acknowledged (access remains a barrier even after role model inspiration; representation in media is necessary but not sufficient; benefits may be short-term unless structural barriers are also addressed); reasoned conclusion.

Secure: Benefits and limitations both present; specific examples used; mostly accurate; conclusion reached.

Developing: Mainly benefits of role models described; limited discussion of limitations; some specific examples.

Emerging: Basic statement that role models are positive with little evaluative content.

Acceptable content in favour: visible high-profile athletes from underrepresented groups inspire identification ('if they can, so can I'); Dame Sarah Storey and Ellie Simmonds have demonstrably increased disabled young people's participation in cycling and swimming; Dina Asher-Smith's success has increased female participation in athletics; role models are low-cost and have wide reach through media. Limitations: role model effect is strongest for those who already have access; if facilities, cost and provision remain barriers, inspiration does not translate to participation; role model effect may be short-lived without sustained media coverage and structural change. Conclusion: role models are a valuable catalyst for increased engagement, but most effective when accompanied by structural changes that make participation practically possible.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which socio-economic group is the most significant factor affecting engagement patterns in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of socio-economic group alongside other factors (gender, age, ethnicity, disability); comparison of relative impact; evidence-based discussion; consistent sporting examples; balanced conclusion that acknowledges socio-economic group as highly significant while recognising other factors are also important.

Secure: Socio-economic group well developed; at least two other factors compared; some evidence; conclusion present.

Developing: Socio-economic group described well but other factors underexplored; limited comparison; argument mainly one-sided.

Emerging: Basic description of socio-economic group as a barrier with little evaluation or comparison.

In favour of socio-economic as most significant: cost is a near-universal barrier (club fees, equipment, transport apply across all sports); lower-income areas often have fewer and lower-quality facilities; education and knowledge of health benefits correlates with participation; time poverty (shift work, multiple jobs) reduces available leisure time for sport.

Other factors challenging primacy: gender stereotyping affects women regardless of income level; disability creates barriers (access, adapted provision) that money alone cannot fully resolve; ethnicity-specific cultural barriers exist independently of income; age-related decline in participation is largely physiological and independent of income. Conclusion: socio-economic group is one of the most pervasive and impactful factors because it affects access to virtually every aspect of sport participation, but no single factor fully explains engagement patterns — the most marginalised individuals typically face multiple overlapping barriers simultaneously.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the 'golden triangle' in sport?
A) The three governing bodies of British sport
B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media
C) The three levels of sport (elite, club, grassroots)
D) The relationship between coach, athlete and official
practice_questions.marks: B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Identify one positive impact and one negative impact of commercialisation on performers.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid positive impact on performers (e.g. high earnings from salary, sponsorship and endorsements / increased media profile enabling social impact / financial security allowing full-time training). 1 mark for any valid negative impact on performers (e.g. increased pressure from sponsors / fixture congestion increasing injury risk / female or disabled athletes in less commercial sports earning far less than male counterparts).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a sport might benefit from increased media coverage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the mechanism by which media coverage benefits sport (e.g. media coverage reaches a large audience, raising the sport's profile); 1 mark for a second mechanism (e.g. increased profile makes the sport more attractive to sponsors, generating funding); 1 mark for applying to a realistic sporting example (e.g. increased Sky Sports coverage of women's football has raised the sport's profile, attracted new sponsors such as Barclays and increased both grassroots participation and professional player salaries).

practice_questions.text: A small national governing body of a minority sport is considering seeking a major commercial sponsorship deal. Discuss the potential advantages and disadvantages for the sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid advantage (e.g. sponsorship funding could improve facilities, develop coaching pathways and support elite programme development). 1 mark for developing the advantage (e.g. with improved facilities and coaching, the sport's competitive standard rises, attracting more media interest and creating a positive feedback loop). 1 mark for a valid disadvantage (e.g. the sponsor may influence the governance of the sport, pressuring it to schedule events at commercially convenient times or to change rules to make it more TV-friendly). 1 mark for developing the disadvantage (e.g. if the sport compromises its character to satisfy commercial demands, it risks alienating its core participants and supporters who value its traditions, potentially reducing long-term participation).

practice_questions.text: Table 2 shows estimated broadcast revenues for three sports in one year: Football: £3.2 billion. Athletics: £48 million. Gymnastics: £12 million. Analyse what this data suggests about the impact of media commercialisation on sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The data is correctly quoted and interpreted; the inequality between sports is analysed; implications for funding, sponsorship and participation are explored; mechanisms of the golden triangle are invoked; consistent evaluation of the impact on under-covered versus well-covered sports; technically accurate language.

Secure: Data read and compared accurately; at least two implications drawn; some golden triangle analysis; generally accurate; mostly applied to the sports named.

Developing: Data read; one or two implications drawn; limited analysis of mechanisms or inequality.

Emerging: Data partially read; basic comments with little analytical structure.

Acceptable content: football's £3.2bn dwarfs athletics (£48m) and gymnastics (£12m) by factors of 67 and 267 respectively; this inequality in broadcast revenue translates to massive inequality in sponsorship income and ultimately in development funding; football can fund global star players and top-class facilities; athletics and gymnastics must rely on national lottery funding, governing body grants and smaller sponsors; the golden triangle reinforces this: football's large audience attracts more sponsors, generating more investment, improving quality, generating more viewers; athletics and gymnastics lack the audience scale to enter this loop; the consequence is that participation growth in minority sports is constrained by lack of funding and visibility, creating a structural disadvantage for any sport that cannot attract large television audiences.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which commercialisation has had a positive impact on sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of positive and negative impacts across multiple stakeholders (sport, performers, spectators, sponsors); examples from different sports; mechanisms of golden triangle discussed; balanced judgement reached with justification.

Secure: Both positive and negative impacts covered across at least two stakeholder groups; specific examples used; conclusion present.

Developing: Mainly positive or mainly negative impacts; limited stakeholder analysis; some examples.

Emerging: Basic list of impacts with little evaluative structure.

Positive: enormous funding enables elite development, improved facilities and global reach; media coverage grows audiences and inspires participation; performers earn financial security; minority sports gain profile during major events; commercial investment has raised the spectacle and quality of sport.
